drills.q: What specific class of bug does E2E testing catch that integration testing structurally cannot, and why?
drills.a: Seam bugs in the actual deployed wiring between components -- e.g. a frontend build pointing at the wrong API version, a broken post-login redirect, or a race condition that only shows up under real network latency between genuinely deployed services. Integration tests prove each side works against a realistic copy of its dependency; only E2E proves the real, currently-deployed wiring is correct.

drills.q: Why did Selenium-era E2E suites earn a reputation for flakiness, mechanically?
drills.a: Selenium had no built-in auto-waiting -- every async UI interaction needed a hand-written explicit wait (e.g. WebDriverWait until element clickable), and missing or mistuning one either raced the page (intermittent failure) or slowed the suite unnecessarily. Combined with manual driver-binary version management and no native parallelism, this produced widespread ad hoc, inconsistent flakiness across large suites.

drills.q: An E2E suite is flaky specifically in CI but passes reliably locally. Walk through the diagnosis and fix.
drills.a: Most likely cause: shared or polluted test data under parallel CI execution, since CI runs specs concurrently against shared staging state in a way a local single-threaded run never stresses; CI resource constraints (CPU throttling, network jitter) can also expose real timing races invisible on a warm local machine. Fix: provision isolated data per test or per parallel worker via direct API calls (not through the UI), and confirm auto-waiting is genuinely in use rather than a hidden manual sleep race before assuming 'CI is just different.'

drills.q: Explain the tradeoff between CSS/XPath locators and role/label-based locators (get_by_role, get_by_label) in terms of maintenance cost.
drills.a: CSS/XPath selectors couple a test to markup structure, so an unrelated visual or structural refactor breaks the test with zero behavioral change -- the largest source of untraceable 'why did this break' maintenance tickets in real E2E suites. Role/label-based locators couple the test to the semantic contract a real user relies on, which is far more stable across refactors and incidentally improves accessibility coverage.

drills.q: What does Playwright's storageState solve, and why is it more than a performance optimization?
drills.a: It captures authenticated session state (cookies, local storage) once and lets subsequent tests start already logged in, instead of driving the full login UI flow per test. Beyond saving time, it removes login -- itself a multi-step async flow -- as a shared source of flakiness across every test that isn't specifically testing the login/auth flow itself.

drills.q: A staff engineer asks you to justify cutting an 80-spec E2E suite down to 15. Give the argument, and the honest counter-risk you should acknowledge.
drills.a: Identify the 15 as the genuinely revenue-critical, cross-system journeys, and show the remaining 65 either duplicate what integration tests already prove or cover low-business-impact paths relative to their measured flakiness and CI runtime cost -- back this with real flake-rate and time data, not a general principle. Counter-risk to acknowledge: one of the cut 65 might catch a real regression later; the honest position is that this trade is usually worth it (a permanently slow, low-trust suite people route around costs more), unless that specific journey's business risk (compliance, revenue exposure) genuinely justifies the ongoing maintenance cost.

drills.q: Explain the E2E 'rot loop' end to end -- what starts it, and where in the loop does the real fix need to be applied?
drills.a: It starts with unisolated shared test data: one test's side effect corrupts another test's assumed state, causing a flaky failure. The team responds by rerunning until green or merging on red, which erodes trust in red E2E builds generally. The suite then grows with more journeys added 'just in case' since testing discipline has already broken down, increasing the flakiness surface and compounding the cycle. The real fix is at the start of the loop -- per-test/per-worker data isolation -- not at the symptom (adding retry logic or telling engineers to stop merging on red).

drills.q: Why should visual regression testing (Percy/Chromatic-style pixel diffing) and functional E2E testing be treated as separate signals even if they share the same browser-automation infrastructure?
drills.a: They catch different bug classes: a checkout flow can visually shift (color, layout) while still functionally completing correctly, or render pixel-identical while being functionally broken. Conflating the two in one report muddies what a red result actually means and routes failures to the wrong owner -- a visual diff typically needs design/product review, a functional failure needs engineering -- slowing triage in both directions.

drills.q: Your company is adopting AI-assisted E2E test generation that can produce dozens of new specs per sprint. What's the risk, and what governance would you apply?
drills.a: Faster spec authoring doesn't change the underlying economics that cause E2E suites to rot -- data isolation, environment strategy, and criticality triage are unaffected by how fast specs are written, so ungoverned AI-generated specs will produce the same large/slow/flaky/ignored suite, just faster. Apply the same criticality rubric (revenue-critical, genuinely cross-system, isolated test data) to AI-generated specs before merge as to human-authored ones, and treat growing auto-generated coverage as a metric to scrutinize rather than celebrate by itself.

drills.q: How do ephemeral per-PR environments change the E2E test-data-isolation problem, and what do they NOT solve?
drills.a: They eliminate cross-PR contention entirely by giving each PR its own full-stack environment and dataset, removing the shared-staging-pollution failure mode that causes many CI-only flaky failures. They do NOT solve intra-PR parallelism -- multiple E2E specs running concurrently within the same PR's environment still need per-test/per-worker data isolation (unique tenants/users), since the ephemeral environment is shared across those parallel specs.
